name: Felix Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get into Northlight Studio around half nine, make a pot of coffee, and look at what the account side has lined up. We're five people in two rooms above a bike shop, and I'm the senior designer, so most identity work starts at my desk. Right now it's a logo and shop signage for a food co-op and a season poster for a small theatre. Every job starts in my sketchbook with a pencil before I touch the screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a mark clicks, when you can shrink a logo to the size of a stamp and it still reads. What wears me out is the endless rounds of tiny changes from clients who want it bigger, then smaller, then back. Priya, who owns the studio, keeps the clients happy, and I keep the work honest. My partner Lena is a nurse on night shifts, so I often eat dinner alone at my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the studio I'd tell the juniors that people still want a human who listens and gets their story. Online I'd probably post something smug about the hype bubble bursting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be nervous, because the cheap end of our work was already leaking away before AI. The co-ops and charities we serve are always short of money, and some of them already use free template sites for flyers. My job looks safe in this world, but the studio's margins are thin and that was true last year too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, sketchbook first, and not touch the AI tools at all. I'd push Priya to put our prices up a little, about five percent, because clients who stay are paying for craft. I'd keep putting a hundred a month into savings, which is all I can manage on our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a small knot underneath. Relief that the thing everybody shouted about came to nothing. The knot is the same one I've had since I started, which is that small studios close all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the template sites. Which clients have you already lost to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the community garden stopped using us for their event posters and did them on a free site instead. They looked fine, a bit flat, but fine is enough for a lot of people. That stung more than I expected, because I'd designed their logo three years ago. Fine is the enemy of good design, and fine is free now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could you manage if the studio did close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about three months of rent and bills put aside, maybe four if Lena covers more. There are a few other studios in the city, so I'd find something, but probably not as senior. I'd hate going back to being a production designer resizing banners all day.

say: I'd say the **hype was overblown** and clients still want a human who listens.
I'd tell the juniors that **craft and listening** are what keep the studio going.
think: I think my job is safe, but **cheap work** was already leaking to template sites.
I worry the studio's **thin margins** could close it even without AI.
do: Keep working **sketchbook first** and refuse to start using AI tools.
Push Priya to raise **prices about five percent** for clients who value craft.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** toward a cushion of three to four months.
feel: He feels **relief** that the hype faded, with an old **knot** about small studios closing.
S0.quote: Fine is the enemy of good design, and fine is free now.
fieldNote: He was already anxious about **template sites** before AI came up, and the garden poster loss still stings.
His public line is **smug**, but privately he worries about the studio's margins.
He refuses AI tools on principle, and treats the **sketchbook** as part of his identity.

steps.text: Keep starting every identity job in the sketchbook, not on screen
Put a hundred a month into savings toward four months' cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice that companies are making, not the weather. At work I'd argue we should be loud about being a human studio. Online I'd share every story about designers being let go and ask who's profiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it eats the middle of my job first. Layouts, resizing, the first round of logo ideas, the copy on a poster, all of that is thinking work a machine could do. Priya would hire fewer juniors and lean on me to check machine work, and I'd be bad at it because I don't use the tools. I could see my hours cut, or my role turned into something I don't recognise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd join the designers' union branch, which I've meant to do for ages, and get Priya to agree a policy on what we tell clients. I'd cut our takeaway nights from three to one a week and get my savings closer to six months. I'd look at a letterpress course at the community print shop, because hands-on printing is slower for robots to reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly, and tired. I chose this work because it felt human, and now I'd be told to babysit a machine. Underneath the anger I'm scared, because I'm not quick with new tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be bad at checking machine work. What would you do if Priya asked you to learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do it, grumbling, because I need the job. But I'd ask for training in work hours, not on my own evenings. I've watched Jonah, our junior, use those tools, and he gets forty logos in a minute and can't tell which one is any good. A machine can make forty logos, but somebody still has to know which logo is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, the junior, first. He's twenty-three and his whole job is the stuff the software does now. I came up doing two years of resizing and it taught me everything, and that ladder just disappears. I'd feel guilty being safe while he gets cut.

say: I'd say job losses are a **choice companies make**, not something like the weather.
I'd argue the studio should market itself loudly as a **human studio**.
think: I think AI eats the **middle of my job** first: layouts, resizing and first ideas.
I expect **fewer juniors** and my role turned into checking machine work.
do: Join the **designers' union** branch this year and push for a studio AI policy.
Cut takeaway nights from **three to one** to build savings toward six months.
Sign up for a **letterpress course** at the community print shop.
feel: He feels **angry** and tired at being asked to babysit a machine.
Underneath, he is **scared** because he is slow with new technology.
S1.quote: A machine can make forty logos, but somebody still has to know which logo is good.
fieldNote: He blames **companies and owners**, not the technology itself, which fits his politics.
He would learn the tools **under protest**, and only on paid time.
The fate of **Jonah (the junior)** worries him more than his own job.

steps.text: Join the local designers' union branch before spring
Build savings from three toward six months of expenses
Take the evening letterpress course at the community print shop
Cut takeaway nights from three a week to one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments let this happen with their eyes shut. I'd be at every protest and I'd write to my representative every week. At the studio I'd say we need to talk about what happens to all five of us, not pretend it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my design job is gone within two years. Screen work is all thinking work, and robots coming three years later doesn't help me because I don't touch anything physical. Northlight would probably close, because why pay us when clients can get a whole brand for the price of a subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first week I'd sit down with Lena and work out what we can live on with just her nursing pay. I'd move my letterpress course from a hobby into a real plan and look for a print shop apprenticeship, since hands-on work gets about three more years. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food, and I'd lean on the union for any legal help with redundancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. Two years is nothing; I've had haircuts that took longer to grow out. I'd feel useless and a bit ashamed that I didn't move sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots coming later doesn't help you. Does it help Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, and that's strange to admit. Nursing is hands-on, so Lena's job has more time than mine, and people will want a human at the bedside for longer. Lena would be keeping us both, which she'd never complain about, but I'd hate it. I'd go from senior designer to the man who cooks dinner for a nurse coming off nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes first, it's eight years old and we barely need it. Then the studio membership I pay for at the print shop, which hurts, but the course is more important. We'd stop talking about a bigger flat for at least a few years.

say: I'd say governments let this happen with their **eyes shut**.
I'd go to **every protest** and write to my representative weekly.
think: I think my design job is **gone within two years**, since it's all screen work.
I expect **Northlight to close** once clients buy a brand by subscription.
do: Work out a budget on **Lena's nursing pay** alone in the first week.
Look for a **print shop apprenticeship**, since hands-on work gets three more years.
Sell the **eight-year-old car** and cut everything but rent and food.
feel: He feels the **floor has gone** and two years is no time at all.
He feels **useless and ashamed** that he didn't move sooner.
S2.quote: I'd go from senior designer to the man who cooks dinner for a nurse coming off nights.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that **screen work** has no robot delay, unlike Lena's nursing.
Losing his status as **breadwinner** stings more than the money itself.
He reaches for **protest and the union** first, then for hands-on print work.

steps.text: Write to his representative every week about job losses
Apply for apprenticeships at local print shops
Sell the eight-year-old car and drop the print studio membership
Live on Lena's nursing pay and use union redundancy help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, just with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get rules in place, so let's use them. At the studio I'd want us to agree what we'd do together if the work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years buys me something, but I still think the design job goes. What changes is that I'm thirty-two when it lands, not twenty-nine, and I could have a trade by then. The robots coming around 2034 means a print trade gives me maybe eight years of work from today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the letterpress course and then do two years of weekends at the print shop to properly learn the presses. I'd save hard, aiming for six months of cover before 2030. I'd also go to union meetings and push for a fund to help designers retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like falling and more like a slow leak. I'd have a plan, which helps, but I'd still lie awake doing sums. It's grief, a bit, for the job I trained six years for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to print. Why that rather than something completely different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my hands already know it, and I don't want to start from nothing at thirty. Ink, paper weight, getting a colour to sit right on cotton stock, that's still design, just with your hands. Rosa at the print shop told me she can't find anyone under fifty who wants to learn. Learning letterpress feels less like giving up design and more like keeping it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lie awake doing sums. What are the sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a print apprentice wage covers my half of the rent, which it doesn't, not quite. Whether we can still have kids one day if I'm earning two-thirds of what I do now. Those are the sums.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get rules in place and should use them.
I'd want the studio to agree a **joint plan** if the work dries up.
think: I think the **design job still goes**, but I'd be thirty-two with a trade.
I think print gives me about **eight years** before robots arrive.
do: Finish the letterpress course, then do **two years of weekends** at the print shop.
Save toward **six months of cover** before 2030.
Push the union for a **retraining fund** for designers.
feel: He feels a **slow leak** rather than a fall, with sleepless sums.
He feels **grief** for the job he trained six years for.
S3.quote: Learning letterpress feels less like giving up design and more like keeping it.
fieldNote: The extra years turn his panic into a **concrete trade plan**.
Money questions reach into **having children**, not just rent.
Even with time, he still expects to **lose the design income**, which keeps him alarmed.

steps.text: Do two years of weekend shifts learning the presses at the print shop
Reach six months of savings before 2030
Push the union branch to set up a designer retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if anyone actually bothers. I'd want shorter weeks and shared gains, not a few companies getting rich. I'd keep saying that loudly at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels almost survivable. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, with a decade of design behind me and maybe a print trade beside it. The worry doesn't go, but it moves further away, and I'm good at ignoring things that are far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep designing at Northlight and not rush. I'd do the letterpress course at an easy pace and maybe sell small print runs at weekend markets. I'd stay in the union and vote for whoever has a real plan for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still a bit sad, because the end point is the same. But I could breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're good at ignoring things far away. Is that a risk here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's exactly my risk. Lena says I'll wake up in 2035 still drawing in the same sketchbook with no plan. She's probably right, so I'd want something on the calendar each year that forces me to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that yearly thing be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every January, I'd book one print market and one course, and pay upfront so I can't back out. Paying upfront is the only way I ever finish anything.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do this properly if anyone bothers.
I'd push for **shorter weeks** and shared gains, not a few rich companies.
think: I think ten years feels **almost survivable**, with a print trade beside design.
I worry I'll **ignore it** because the danger feels far away.
do: Keep designing at Northlight and take the **letterpress course** slowly.
Sell small **print runs** at weekend markets.
Book and **prepay** one course and one market every January.
feel: He feels **steadier** and able to breathe.
He is still a little **sad** because the end point is the same.
S4.quote: Paying upfront is the only way I ever finish anything.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **breathe**, but he still expects the design job to end.
He knows his own habit of **putting things off**, and Lena calls it out.
He chooses a **prepaid commitment** each January to beat his own resistance.

steps.text: Keep designing at Northlight without rushing a move
Sell small letterpress print runs at weekend markets
Vote for candidates with a real plan for displaced designers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because two years is nowhere near enough to learn a trade. What would help is paid retraining with a living wage while you learn, not a voucher for an online course. And some kind of support for small studios so they don't all shut in the same year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we lose that isn't money. A logo for a food co-op is a small thing, but it's somebody's dream on a sign above a door. I don't want a world where a human made the dream and a machine made the sign above the door.

headlineQuote: I don't want a world where a human made the dream and a machine made the sign above the door.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old senior designer** at Northlight, a five-person studio doing identities for co-ops and theatres.
He works **sketchbook first**, never uses AI, and lives with Lena, a night-shift nurse.
He blames **companies and governments**, and turns to the union and protest when work is threatened.
His fallback in every scenario is **letterpress printing**, because hands-on work gives him more time.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and only partly relaxes with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to learn a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a living wage while learning, not online course vouchers.
Support so **small studios** don't all close in the same year.
